title: Tenant-island breaker with safe fanout and evaluation playbook
creator: Laura Chen
description:
Goal: Implement a tenant-island circuit breaker that prevents a noisy or malfunctioning tenant (or tenant -> model/dependency path) from cascading into global capacity problems, while providing safe, observable fallback options and SLO-aligned degradation.

Scope and constraints:
- Per-tenant + per-dependency + per-model breakers with shared config surface but independent state and quotas.
- Must integrate with the routing/fallback orchestration layer (fanout controller) and Console for observability and rollouts.
- Keep latency SLOs and throughput targets as first-class inputs to trip logic; avoid brittle static thresholds.
- Support cross-region failover: breaker decisions are local to the region but expose signals for global coordinator to decide region-level evacuation.

Design summary (high-level):
1) Scoring-based trip decision (adaptive): compute a short-window stability score S for each {tenant, dependency, model} key where
   S = w_e * (err_rate / err_slo) + w_l * (p95_latency / lat_slo) + w_q * (queue_depth / queue_budget)
   - default weights: w_e=0.6, w_l=0.3, w_q=0.1 (configurable per tenant class)
   - err_slo and lat_slo pulled from tenant's SLO profile in the Console
   - use exponentially-weighted moving averages over request-count windows (min 1k requests or 60s) to stabilize short bursts
   - trip when S > 1.15 for two consecutive windows OR when an absolute emergency condition is hit (error rate > 30% over 10s)

2) Tenant-Island behavior:
   - When a tenant trips, route only that tenant's traffic into degraded paths (isolation), do not reduce global capacity for other tenants.
   - Keep a small emergency credit pool (configurable) to allow low-rate probes to verify recovery (see recovery/hysteresis).

3) Safe fallback tiering (ordered list of fallback actions):
   - Tier A: Route to model variant with lower compute (quantized or smaller arch) in same region (fastest, cheapest fallback).
   - Tier B: Apply aggressive request-level degradation: reduce max_tokens, remove optional tool-calls or long-context retrievals.
   - Tier C: Serve from a per-tenant short-term cache if available (prefix/KV cache or last-good response) with cache-control metadata.
   - Tier D: Queue requests with Retry-After hint and a lightweight 202-accepted response + webhook/callback option.
   - Tier E: Proxy to per-tenant degraded synthetic handler that returns structured minimal outputs and deterministic failure codes.
   - Tier F: (last resort) Spill to cross-region compatible region if policy permits and latency budget allows.

4) Hysteresis & recovery:
   - Minimum cool-down window after trip: 30s to 2m (configurable by tenant class).
   - Recovery probes: allow 1 probe per 5s initially, ramp to 1% of normal rate over 5m if probes succeed.
   - Re-arm only after score S falls below 0.85 for 3 consecutive windows and no emergency flags in recent 2m.

5) Capacity credits & graceful throttling:
   - Each tenant has a rolling credit bank representing recently unused capacity. Trip thresholds and fallback aggressiveness should factor in available credits.
   - If credits exhausted, escalate fallback tiers quicker and increase Retry-After suggestions.

6) Observability & dashboards:
   - Console panels per-tenant: S score timeline, contributors (errors, latency, queue), fallback tier activations, throughput, and credit balance.
   - Alerts: Pager at P0 only if system-level global capacity risk (e.g., >5% of nodes affected or >3 tenants in island state simultaneously);
     otherwise create an Ops ticket (P1) and alert on-call for the tenant-owner if labeled enterprise.
   - Audit logs: all breaker state transitions (trip, probe, recover, manual override) must emit structured audit entries with causation links.

7) Testing and verification:
   - Unit tests for scoring logic and window semantics.
   - Integration tests that simulate tenant spike, slow dependency, and region outage; assert other tenants unaffected.
   - Chaos test: run synthetic noisy-tenant experiments in staging to validate islanding and recovery ramps.
   - Performance: breaker evaluation path must add <1ms p95 CPU overhead per request at 100k RPS.

Rollout plan:
- Phase 0 (lab): implement scoring engine and fallback hooks behind a feature-flag; run internal fuzz tests.
- Phase 1 (staging): enable for 5 non-prod tenants, verify dashboards and recovery probes.
- Phase 2 (canary): enable for 1% of production traffic (low-risk tenants first), monitor for 48h.
- Phase 3: graduated ramp to 50% tenants in 2w with rollback plan; require incident runbook for manual overrides.

Open design trade-offs and questions:
- Should we prefer latency-weighted trips for low-latency SLO tenants even if error rates are low? (current approach supports tenant-specific weights.)
- How to encode enterprise contracts that forbid certain fallback tiers (e.g., no cross-region spill, no model-variant switching)? Will require per-tenant policy enforcement in routing layer.
- Backpressure vs. queuing: long queues preserve request semantics but increase memory; we propose small soft-queue + Retry-After hybrid.

Implementation checklist:
- [x] Scoring engine prototype (in Rust runtime shim) — initial commit: GH: redwood/runtime#1456
- [x] Console SLO binding and UI mockups — Confluence: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/OPS/pages/tenant-island-design
- [ ] Fallback action adapters (model routing, cache read, queue accept/response)
- [ ] Audit/logging plumbing to event bus and Console
- [ ] Canary rollout automation and kill-switch endpoint
- [ ] Integration and chaos tests

Success criteria for GA:
- No customer-facing error-rate regression attributable to breaker in first 30 days of rollout.
- Mean time to re-enable a legitimately recovered tenant < 3m via automated probes (or < 5m with manual intervention).
- Observatory coverage: 95% of breaker transitions have linked traces and at least one explanatory signal (latency or error histogram).
